cards.question: A loop has a battery and three bulbs in series. Where is the current smallest?
options: Nowhere: it's the same all the way round
cards.why: In a single loop the current is the same at every point. The bulbs take energy from it, not current.

cards.question: Why does a lamp light the instant you close the switch, though electrons drift less than a millimetre a second?
options: The wire is already full of charge, and the push travels almost at the speed of light
The battery fires electrons down the wire very fast
The lamp stores charge from last time
cards.why: Every electron in the loop starts drifting at once, because the push travels round the whole loop almost instantly.

cards.question: What does "5 V at this point" mean on a schematic?
cards.why: Voltage is always between two points. A voltage given at one point is measured from ground.

cards.question: Your meter is in amps mode and you touch the probes across a lamp. What happens?
options: It shorts the lamp out and probably blows the meter's fuse
cards.why: In amps mode a meter is nearly a plain wire. To read current it has to go in a break in the loop.

cards.question: You need 12 V to push 25 mA through a resistor. Which do you fit?
cards.why: R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 0.025 = 480 Ω, and 470 Ω is the nearest standard value.

cards.question: Why do filament bulbs usually fail just as they're switched on?
options: A cold filament has low resistance, so it takes a surge of current
The voltage is higher at switch-on
cards.why: Cold tungsten resists about a tenth as much as hot, so for an instant the current is several times normal.

cards.question: What do two parts in parallel always share?
cards.why: Both their ends are joined, so they have the same voltage across them. The current splits between them.

cards.question: What do two parts in series always share?
cards.why: There's only one path, so the same current goes through both. The voltage splits between them.

cards.question: Three wires meet. 40 mA flows in on one and 15 mA out on another. What flows on the third?
cards.why: What flows into a junction flows out: 40 in, so 40 out in all, and 40 − 15 = 25 mA goes out on the third.

cards.question: You put a 10 kΩ resistor in parallel with a 1 kΩ. The pair is…
cards.why: Each parallel path is another way through, so the pair is less than the smallest: about 909 Ω.

cards.question: Why not put a fresh battery in parallel with a flat one?
options: Current flows from the fresh one into the flat one
The voltages add and overload the circuit
cards.why: The fresh battery pushes current back into the flat one, wasting charge and warming both. Big batteries can do it hard enough to be dangerous.

cards.question: A string of parts has stopped working. Across which part will you read the full supply voltage?
options: The one with the break in it
cards.why: With no current, nothing else drops any voltage, so all of it appears across the break.

cards.question: Two equal resistors in series across 9 V. What's at the point between them, unloaded?
cards.why: Equal resistors share the voltage equally. Out = 9 × R ÷ (R + R) = 4.5 V.

cards.question: Why does a divider's output fall when you connect a load?
options: The load in parallel makes the bottom resistance smaller
cards.why: Two resistances in parallel are less than either, so the bottom's share of the voltage shrinks.

cards.question: What does a stiffer divider cost you?
options: More current, wasted all the time
cards.why: Lower resistances carry more current, whether the load is there or not.

cards.question: A source reads 12 V open and 11 V while delivering 0.5 A. What's its inside resistance?
cards.why: It lost 1 V inside at 0.5 A: 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2 Ω.

cards.question: To keep a signal's voltage, feed it into…
cards.why: A high input impedance pulls little current, so the source hardly sags.

cards.question: Measured open, shorted and loaded, a solar panel's points…
options: bend: it holds its voltage, then collapses
cards.why: A panel is close to a current source in parallel with diodes, not a voltage behind a resistor.

cards.question: Three times the current through a resistor means how much heat?
cards.why: P = I² × R, so 3² = 9 times.

cards.question: A 24 V, 100 Ah battery holds…
cards.why: Watt-hours = volts × amp-hours: 24 × 100 = 2400 Wh.

cards.question: Why do larger off-grid systems run at 48 V rather than 12 V?
options: A quarter of the current, so a sixteenth of the cable loss
cards.why: The same power at four times the voltage needs a quarter of the current; I² × R falls sixteenfold.

cards.question: What does a fuse protect?
cards.why: It must blow before the cable overheats: above the load's current, below the cable's rating.

cards.question: A load matched to its source's inside resistance gets the most power. What's the catch?
options: Half the energy is wasted inside the source
cards.why: At the match, the inside resistance and the load share the power equally. Power systems want a load much bigger than the inside resistance.

cards.question: How do you find a high-resistance joint?
options: Measure the voltage across it with the current flowing
Measure its resistance with the power off
cards.why: Under load a bad joint drops volts. With no current it drops nothing, and a meter's tiny test current may not show it.

cards.question: A wave repeats every 10 ms. Its frequency is…
cards.why: Frequency is one over the period: 1 ÷ 0.01 s = 100 Hz.

cards.question: A signal swings 0.4 V each way around its middle. Its peak to peak is…
cards.why: Bottom to top is twice the amplitude.

cards.question: A stage on 12 V can swing from 1 V to 11 V. Where should its steady voltage sit?
cards.why: Halfway between the limits gives the same headroom up and down.

cards.question: The bottoms of a wave come out flat, the tops don’t. The steady voltage is…
cards.why: The wave runs into the bottom limit first, so it sits too close to it. Raise the steady voltage.

cards.question: A guitar note at 110 Hz also has quieter sines at…
cards.why: Harmonics are at whole multiples of the note; their mix is the instrument’s tone.

cards.question: A pedal passes no sound. Its buffer’s input should sit at 4.5 V and reads 9 V. Most likely…
options: the resistor pulling it down is open
cards.why: The input has gone to the top: whatever should pull it down to the middle isn’t. A flat battery would make it lower, not 9 V.

cards.question: 10 kΩ and 100 µF have a time constant of…
A capacitor charges with τ = 2 s. When is it nearly full?
cards.why: About five time constants: 10 s. After one, it is only 63% of the way.

cards.question: In a circuit that has settled, how much current flows through a capacitor?
options: The same as through the resistor before it
cards.why: Once it has charged to the steady voltage, nothing more flows. Only changes pass.

cards.question: R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF in a low-pass filter. The corner is about…
Turning a tone knob that raises R in a low-pass filter makes the sound…
cards.why: A bigger R lowers the corner, so more of the highs are cut.

cards.question: You switch off a relay coil. Across the switch there is, for an instant…
options: a spike far above the supply voltage
cards.why: The coil’s field keeps the current going and drives whatever voltage it takes, until the field is spent.

cards.question: A conducting silicon diode drops about…
cards.why: Past its knee, a silicon diode holds about 0.6 to 0.7 V whatever the current.

cards.question: A red LED (2 V) on 12 V at 10 mA needs a resistor of about…
Why can’t you run an LED straight from a 3 V battery that “matches” its voltage?
options: A little extra voltage makes a lot of current, so nothing sets it
cards.why: Past the knee the current climbs steeply. A resistor is what sets the current.

cards.question: Warm a silicon diode by 50 °C. Its forward voltage…
cards.why: About 2 mV less for every degree warmer.

cards.question: A 50 Hz half-wave rectifier feeds 10 mA from 1000 µF. The ripple is about…
Which clipping diodes let the most signal through before they clip?
cards.why: LEDs have the highest knee, near 2 V, so they clip later and louder.
